title: TCP and TLS
summary: How a connection is set up, how TCP recovers lost data, and how TLS adds encryption, counted in round trips.

blocks.p: The internet moves data in small packets, and it makes no promises about them. A packet can be lost, duplicated, or arrive after a packet sent later. Anyone on the path can also read it.

Applications need the opposite: every byte, in order, readable only by the other end. **TCP** gives you the reliable, ordered stream. **TLS** runs on top of TCP and adds encryption and proof of who the server is.
Both need a few messages back and forth before the first byte of your request can go. Each exchange costs a round trip, so setup time grows with distance.

Before sending data, the two ends agree on starting sequence numbers. The client sends a **SYN**, the server answers with a **SYN-ACK**, and the client confirms with an **ACK**. This is the three-way handshake in [RFC 9293](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293#section-3.5). It costs one round trip before the client can send data.

TLS then agrees on encryption keys. The server sends a **certificate**, which proves it owns the name the client asked for. The handshake ends with a **Finished** message from each side, which checks that nobody changed the messages in between.

TLS 1.2 needs two round trips for a full handshake. [TLS 1.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446) needs one, because the client sends its key share in its first message instead of waiting to learn what the server supports.

blocks.caption: Opening an HTTPS connection with TLS 1.2, with TLS 1.3, and resuming a TLS 1.3 session with 0-RTT data.

blocks.p: With **0-RTT**, a client that has talked to the server before can send its request in its first TLS message. [RFC 8446](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446#section-8) warns that an attacker can replay 0-RTT data, so it suits only requests that are safe to repeat.
TCP numbers every byte. The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects. If a segment goes missing, the sender notices that its bytes were never acknowledged and sends them again.

The receiver must hand bytes to the application in order. Bytes that arrive after a gap wait in a buffer until the gap is filled. This is called **head-of-line blocking**, and it matters again in the HTTP lesson.

blocks.caption: Bytes 1001 to 2000 are lost. Bytes 2001 to 3000 arrive but wait until the missing bytes are sent again.

list: **Reuse connections.** A connection that is already open skips both handshakes. HTTP/1.1 keeps connections open by default, as [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-9.3) describes.
**Terminate TLS close to users.** The handshake costs round trips to whoever ends the TLS connection. A CDN or load balancer near the user can do that, which shortens each round trip.
**QUIC merges the two handshakes.** HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which sets up transport and TLS 1.3 encryption together in one round trip, as [RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001) describes.
**Certificates expire.** A server's certificate is valid for a fixed period. An expired certificate makes browsers refuse the connection, so renew certificates automatically.

blocks.p: Set the round trip time and the TLS version, and see how long the client waits before the first byte of the response.

blocks.caption: Time to the first byte of a response on a new connection, ignoring server work.

list: TCP turns lost, reordered packets into a reliable, ordered stream of bytes.
The TCP handshake costs one round trip. TLS 1.2 adds two more, TLS 1.3 adds one.
A lost segment holds up every byte behind it until it is sent again.
Reusing open connections avoids the handshakes entirely.
